newsitem.title: USA: NYS approves contingency pact despite opposition.
newsitem.headline: NYS approves contingency pact despite opposition.

text.p: New York State's Senate and Assembly, recognizing that the state's budget again would be late, said Thursday they had approved a $9.65 billion contingency budget to keep the government running through May 9.

But a battle broke out late Wednesday night in the Assembly, which is led by Democrats. Minority Republicans accused the majority party of quashing debate while the Assembly Speaker, Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, said his opponents had tried to stage a filibuster to prevent the pact from being approved.

"A tactic reminiscent of Newt Gingrich's ill-fated effort to derail the federal government two years ago was beaten back by Assembly Democrats," said Silver, referring to the U.S. House Speaker, a Georgia Republican, in a prepared statement.

Silver added that if the contingency pact had been tied up, aid payments to financially stressed municipalities, school districts and elderly individuals who get healthcare benefits would have been late.
The Assembly Republicans saw events very differently, saying Silver had ended debate precipitously.

"Everywhere across the world, communism and tyranny are giving way to liberty and free speech," said Minority Leader Thomas Reynolds, R-Concord, in prepared remarks."Everywhere, that is, except the New York State Assembly."
The New York State Senate, which is controlled by Republicans, took the opportunity to attack the Assembly for approving its own budget, a tack the senate followed last year.

Saying the Assembly's budget would raise spending by more than $5 billion, Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, in prepared remarks, said: "They haven't said how they would pay for their spending increase, but it would probably require a massive tax increase that would wipe out the tremendous economic progress we've made in the past two years."

The Assembly, which has forecast that the state will get as much as $1.6 billion of extra revenues by the end of its 1998 fiscal year, says its budget is balanced, and only raises spending by $2 billion.
